The Scope of UCC Article 2 Revisited 
As a comparison of the court's analysis in Dickinson v. Dodds with 
UCC § 2-205 reveals, it can make a great deal of difference whether a 
contract is governed by the common law or by Article 2 of the Uniform 
Commercial Code. Section 5 of this Chapter, focusing on UCC § 2-207, 
provides 
a dramatic 
example 
of the difference 
between 
traditional 
common law rules and those in Article 2, and each subsequent Chapter 
provides examples of differences 
as well. Thus, analysis 
of many issues 
raised by a contract typically 
starts with a determination 
of whether 
resolution of the issue is governed by Article 2 or by general contract law. 
Accordingly, a good understanding 
of the scope of Article 2 is important. 
As seen previously, the title of Article 2 is "Sales", and the Article 
applies to "transactions in goods." UCC §§ 2-101, 2-102. "Goods," as also 
noted previously, is a defined term. UCC § 2-105. At one level, then, the 
scope determination 
is trivial-if 
the contract in question is one for the 
sale of goods, Article 2 applies; if it is not, general contract law rules will 
apply. But transactions 
are 
often not as simple 
as this dichotomy 
suggests. Rather, many transactions 
involve both goods and something 
else (either services or other property). Consider three examples: 
1. 
Customer 
goes to Store to acquire a window 
air conditioner. 
Customer and Store agree that customer will pay Store $500 in exchange 
for the air conditioner and delivery and installation 
of it by Store.

Customer pays $150 for a GPS navigation 
device. Under the
